Card error, copied as is: hen-house says Lewis & Short has only the adjective gallīnārius and the noun is Traupman’s. Lewis & Short s.v. gallinarius has gallīnārium, ii, n., a hen-house, hen-coop (Col. 8.3.1; Plin. 17.51), so the noun is classical. The period is left modern, as the card has it, until the comment is corrected.
Card error, carried as is: entry-210’s link “Lewis & Short: Abellana” points to logeion …/castanea (the chestnut); it is on hazelnut. Lewis & Short has Abellāna nux (or Avellana) under Abella.
tuna: Lewis & Short’s headword is thunnus, with thynnus as its variant, so the card’s thynnus departs from Lewis & Short’s headword as well as from Traupman’s thunnus; the note says so.
pīpilō set late: Lewis & Short’s only classical citation is Catull. 3.10 on the older reading (pīpilābat) that the card itself rejects for pīpiābat; what remains is the Anthologia Latina.

Forms from the Carmen dē Philomēlā (crocitō, cūcūriō, tetrinniō, mintriō, bombītāre) are set late, as the card calls the poem; its date is uncertain. crocitō is avoid on entry-509’s “not recommended”, although entry-205 lists it neutrally; cūcūriō stays alternative because the card does not say not to use it, though by the card’s own reasoning it is in the same case as crocitāre.

entry-509’s “not recommended” note: quack, hoot and cackle are records recommending clāmat (strīdet as alternative), as the note says for ducks, owls and geese, each with Traupman’s form as avoid. Squeak has no recommended word on the card, so mintriō is an avoid term on mouse.

Periods set by judgement: horīzōn post-classical (Macrobius, non-Christian), though the card calls it late; arcus caelestis modern (not in Lewis & Short; Traupman, M-O); nivis cāsus modern (Traupman; it may be Livy’s, 21.35.6 nivis etiam casus, not checked here); temperature recommends calor (modern in this sense, M-O), since the card calls it the safer word, though the card lists temperātūra first. Uncited phrases are set classical on the cards’ “Ancient” tags, with no citation for the phrase in Lewis & Short: caudam movēre, ōs contrahere, in sale condere, in dorsō natāre, sale pipereque aspergere, laurī folia, aqua salsa. salt-cod is ours: Libellus IV’s description of bacalhau.
Departures the card does not explain, so no note: bālaena (Traupman 145 prints balaena; the card follows Lewis & Short); vibrissae (Lewis & Short marks the i doubtful).
stēlla (star, starfish): the card calls it the series spelling and Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked; the note can give only that, so a ruling with the evidence may be wanted.

Examples placed by judgement: “Nucēs Octōbrī…” is on crack-a-nut, the only record of the batch with nux (it would sit better on entry-112’s nut or walnut); the woodpecker dialogue is on beak; “Ave, ecce avēs!…” is on bird.

Where the card glosses one Latin word with two English words, the second is in also rather than a record of its own: pigeon (dove), gnat (mosquito), moth (cockroach), grasshopper (cricket), glow-worm (firefly), tortoise (turtle), cod (hake), swamp (marsh), bay-sea (gulf). Likewise the narrower forms with their own gloss: doe, mare, sow, billy goat, she-wolf, bay leaves, swim on one’s back.

Domain kept natura for concepts that plainly belong elsewhere: salt, vinegar, mustard, sprinkle, season-food, olive-oil, bitter, raw, unripe, big (culina or sermo); basket (domus); cartilage, pucker (corpus); swim (ludi, with swimming).

Records whose word the card cites no source for carry the card’s libellī line, its only general source: feather, sparrow, fan-its-tail, tail, wag, sheep, horse, hiss, lion, roar, horse-mackerel, cartilage, sunfish, sea-dragon, fig, preserve-in-salt, clove, nutmeg, pucker.
